periodic.heading: The ten elements that matter for orgo
points: C (4 bonds), N (3), O (2), H and the halogens F/Cl/Br/I (1 each). S behaves like O (2), P like N (3).
Bonds formed = 8 − group electrons, except carbon, which shares all four.
Valence electrons: group 1-2 → 1-2. Groups 13-18 → group number minus 10.
B is the odd one out: it forms 3 bonds and is stable with only 6 electrons.

periodic.heading: Two master trends
points: Electronegativity and ionization energy both increase UP and to the RIGHT.
Atomic radius increases DOWN and to the LEFT — the exact opposite.
Why: across a period, more protons pull the same shell tighter. Down a group, you add whole new shells.

periodic.heading: Orbitals & electron configuration — the 5-minute refresher
points: An orbital is a region holding at most 2 electrons (opposite spins). s orbitals are spheres; p orbitals are two-lobed dumbbells, three per shell at right angles.
Filling order for everything orgo cares about: 1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p. Carbon: 1s² 2s² 2p². Nitrogen: …2p³. Oxygen: …2p⁴.
Equal-energy orbitals fill one electron at a time before pairing (Hund's rule).
Valence electrons = the outermost shell. Core electrons just shield. The octet is literally the second shell filled: 2s² + 2p⁶ = 8.
Hybridization is mixing 2s with 2p: one s + three p → four sp³; one s + two p → three sp² plus a leftover p orbital. That leftover p is what makes pi bonds.

periodic.heading: Electronegativity ordering — the mnemonic
points: FUNNY OWLS NEED CLEAN CLOTHES, SOCKS, HATS → F, O, N, Cl, C, S, H — most electronegative to least.

Two caveats the mnemonic glosses over: Cl is very slightly ABOVE N (3.16 vs 3.04), and S is very slightly above C (2.58 vs 2.55). Both pairs are close enough to treat as ties — just do not claim N beats Cl on an exam.
What the mnemonic gets right is the part that matters: F and O dominate, C and H sit at the bottom, and everything organic happens in between.
The payoff: O and N are much more electronegative than C, which is why C-O and C-N bonds are polar, and why those carbons are the electrophilic ones.

polarity.heading: The ordering to have memorized
points: FUNNY OWLS NEED CLEAN CLOTHES, SOCKS, HATS → F > O > N > Cl > C > S > H.
Strictly, Cl edges out N and S edges out C, but both pairs are near-ties. The mnemonic is reliable everywhere else.
Every polarity question reduces to this list: whichever atom sits earlier takes the electrons and carries the delta-minus.
C-H is the one to internalize as effectively NONPOLAR (2.55 vs 2.20). That is why hydrocarbons are greasy and water-insoluble.

polarity.heading: Reading a polar bond
points: The more electronegative atom takes the electron density and gets δ−. Its partner gets δ+.
The dipole arrow points TOWARD the δ− atom (toward the electronegative end).
δ+ carbons are electrophilic — that is where nucleophiles attack. This is the whole basis of orgo reactivity.

polarity.heading: Classifying by ΔEN
points: ΔEN < 0.4 → nonpolar covalent (C–H at 0.35 counts as effectively nonpolar).
ΔEN 0.4 – 1.7 → polar covalent (C–O, C–N, C–Cl).
ΔEN > 1.7 → ionic (Na–Cl).
These are soft boundaries, not hard rules — the ranking matters more than the exact number.

polarity.heading: Bond polarity vs MOLECULAR polarity
points: A polar bond is about two atoms. A polar MOLECULE is about whether all the bond dipoles cancel once you account for shape.
Symmetric shapes cancel: linear with identical ends (CO2), trigonal planar (BF3), tetrahedral with four identical groups (CCl4), octahedral (SF6).
CCl4 is the case to remember: four strongly polar C-Cl bonds, zero net dipole. Polar bonds do NOT guarantee a polar molecule.
Two things break the symmetry. A lone pair on the central atom (H2O bent, NH3 pyramidal, SO2 bent) or outer atoms that are not all the same (CHCl3, CH2Cl2).
Linear does not automatically mean nonpolar: HCN is linear but its two ends differ, so nothing cancels.
This is what decides the intermolecular force: no net dipole means dispersion only, however polar the individual bonds are.

lewis.heading: Building a Lewis structure
points: Count total valence electrons (add one per negative charge, subtract one per positive charge).
Connect the atoms with single bonds, then distribute remaining electrons as lone pairs to the outer atoms first.
If the central atom is short of an octet, convert lone pairs into double or triple bonds.
Check every atom's formal charge at the end.

lewis.heading: Formal charge
points: FC = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − ½(bonding electrons).
Equivalently: FC = valence − lone pair electrons − number of bonds.
Neutral patterns: C with 4 bonds, N with 3 bonds + 1 lone pair, O with 2 bonds + 2 lone pairs.
N with 4 bonds → +1. O with 3 bonds → +1. O with 1 bond + 3 lone pairs → −1. C with 3 bonds and no lone pair → +1.

lewis.heading: Octet exceptions to expect
points: B and Al are commonly stable with 6 electrons (BF₃, AlCl₃) — they are strong Lewis acids because of it.
Third-row elements and below (S, P, Cl) can expand past 8 (SF₆, PCl₅).
Radicals have an odd electron and cannot satisfy every octet.

vsepr.heading: Count GROUPS, not bonds
points: An electron group is any attached atom OR any lone pair.
A double or triple bond counts as ONE group, not two or three. This is the most common mistake.
CO₂ has two groups on carbon (two double bonds) and is therefore linear.

vsepr.heading: Groups → geometry → hybridization
points: 2 groups → linear, 180°, sp
3 groups → trigonal planar, 120°, sp²
4 groups → tetrahedral, 109.5°, sp³
Hybridization follows the group count directly — no lone pair bookkeeping needed.

vsepr.heading: Electron geometry vs molecular shape
points: Electron geometry counts everything, lone pairs included.
Molecular shape describes only where the ATOMS are.
4 groups, 0 lone pairs → tetrahedral. 4 groups, 1 lone pair → trigonal pyramidal (NH₃). 4 groups, 2 lone pairs → bent (H₂O).
Lone pairs repel harder than bonds, so each one squeezes the bond angle a few degrees below ideal.

vsepr.heading: Sigma vs pi
points: Single bond = 1 sigma. Double = 1 sigma + 1 pi. Triple = 1 sigma + 2 pi.
Sigma bonds come from head-on overlap and allow free rotation.
Pi bonds come from sideways p-orbital overlap and LOCK rotation — this is why alkenes have cis/trans isomers.

acidbase.heading: Definitions
points: Bronsted-Lowry: acid donates a proton, base accepts one.
Lewis: acid accepts an electron pair, base donates one. This is the more useful definition for mechanisms.
Conjugate base = acid minus H⁺. Conjugate acid = base plus H⁺.

acidbase.heading: pKa is the whole game
points: Lower pKa = stronger acid. A difference of 1 pKa unit is a factor of 10.
The weaker the acid, the STRONGER its conjugate base.
Equilibrium always favours the side with the weaker acid (higher pKa). This single rule predicts direction for any proton transfer.

acidbase.heading: Anchor pKa values
points: HCl −7 · H₃O⁺ −1.7 · HF 3.2 · carboxylic acid 4.8 · ammonium 9-10 · phenol 10 · thiol 10.5
water 15.7 · alcohol 16 · ketone α-H 19 · terminal alkyne 25 · ammonia 38 · alkene 44 · alkane 50

acidbase.heading: What makes an acid strong (stabilize the conjugate base)
points: Resonance: spreading the negative charge over several atoms. Carboxylic acid vs alcohol is the classic case.
Electronegativity: negative charge is more stable on a more electronegative atom.
Size / polarizability: down a group, bonds weaken and the anion gets more stable — HI is far stronger than HF.
Induction: nearby electron-withdrawing groups pull charge away and stabilize it.

imf.heading: The three forces, strongest to weakest (at similar size)
points: Hydrogen bonding: needs H bonded to N, O, or F. Strongest per-contact force between neutral molecules.
Dipole-dipole: any polar molecule. The δ+ of one molecule attracts the δ− of the next.
London dispersion: every molecule has it, from momentary electron fluctuations. Scales with size and surface area — in big molecules it dominates everything.
These act BETWEEN molecules. Covalent bonds act WITHIN them and are ~10-100× stronger. Boiling breaks IMFs, never bonds.

imf.heading: Hydrogen bonding, precisely
points: Donor: an H attached to N, O, or F. C–H hydrogens never donate.
Acceptor: a lone pair on N, O, or F.
Alcohols donate AND accept. Ethers and carbonyls only accept — which is why butan-1-ol boils at 118 °C while its isomer diethyl ether boils at 35 °C.
Carboxylic acids pair into doubly hydrogen-bonded dimers, boiling even higher.

imf.heading: Predicting boiling points
points: First compare size (dispersion), then the strongest force available.
Same size, add H-bonding → much higher bp: butane 0 °C vs butan-1-ol 118 °C.
Same formula, more branching → lower bp: pentane 36 °C vs neopentane 10 °C (less surface contact).
Bigger halogen, stronger dispersion: F₂ gas → Cl₂ gas → Br₂ liquid → I₂ solid.

imf.heading: Solubility: like dissolves like
points: Polar/H-bonding dissolves polar; nonpolar dissolves nonpolar. Hexane and water do not mix.
Small alcohols (≤4-5 carbons) are water-miscible; beyond that the hydrocarbon tail wins.
Every extraction and recrystallization decision in orgo lab is this rule applied.

skeletal.heading: Reading line-angle drawings
points: Every vertex and every free line end is a carbon atom.
Carbons and their hydrogens are never drawn — each carbon silently carries whatever hydrogens it needs to reach 4 bonds.
Hydrogens on N, O, and other heteroatoms ARE drawn explicitly.
H count on a carbon = 4 − (bonds you can see). A double bond counts as two of those bonds.

skeletal.heading: Degrees of unsaturation
points: Degrees of unsaturation = rings + pi bonds.
From a formula: DoU = (2C + 2 + N − H − X) / 2
A benzene ring is 4 degrees: one ring plus three double bonds.

functional.heading: The carbonyl family — all differ by what is on the C=O carbon
points: Nothing else (just H or C) → aldehyde (at a chain end) or ketone (in the middle).
–OH → carboxylic acid.  –OR → ester.  –NR₂ → amide.  –Cl → acyl chloride.
This one pattern accounts for most of the functional groups you will meet.

functional.heading: The rest
points: Alcohol (–OH), thiol (–SH), amine (–NH₂), ether (C–O–C), alkyl halide (C–X).
Alkene (C=C), alkyne (C≡C), aromatic ring, nitrile (C≡N).
Ether vs alcohol: an ether oxygen has carbon on BOTH sides.

nomenclature.heading: The four steps
points: 1. Find the LONGEST continuous carbon chain — it does not have to be drawn straight.
2. Number it from the end that gives the lowest locants (the suffix group wins first).
3. Name and number every substituent.
4. Assemble: locants-prefixes + parent + suffix, prefixes in alphabetical order.

nomenclature.heading: Stems
points: 1 meth · 2 eth · 3 prop · 4 but · 5 pent · 6 hex · 7 hept · 8 oct · 9 non · 10 dec
Suffix -ane (all single bonds), -ene (double bond), -yne (triple bond), -ol (alcohol).

nomenclature.heading: Details that get marked wrong
points: Alphabetize by the substituent's own name — di/tri/tetra do NOT count (ethyl comes before dimethyl).
Every substituent keeps its own number, even duplicates: 2,2-dimethyl, never 2-dimethyl.
A double bond is numbered by its FIRST carbon: hex-2-ene means the bond spans C2–C3.
An –OH outranks halogens and double bonds when choosing the numbering direction.

resonance.heading: What resonance is
points: One real molecule with delocalized electrons — NOT two species interconverting.
Use the double-headed arrow ↔ between structures. Equilibrium arrows ⇌ mean something completely different.
Only electrons move: pi bonds and lone pairs. If an atom moved, it is a different molecule.

resonance.heading: Ranking contributors
points: 1. Maximize full octets — the strongest factor by far.
2. Minimize the number of formal charges.
3. Put negative charge on the most electronegative atom (and positive on the least).
4. Avoid like charges on adjacent atoms.
Equivalent structures contribute equally and give the most stabilization.

resonance.heading: Why it matters
points: Delocalization = stabilization. It explains carboxylate acidity, allylic cation stability, and benzene.
Requires conjugation: a continuous chain of parallel p orbitals. An sp³ carbon breaks it.

arrows.heading: Reading curved arrows
points: Arrows track ELECTRONS, always drawn from electron-rich to electron-poor.
The TAIL sits on the electron source: a lone pair or a bond — never on an atom symbol or a positive charge.
The HEAD points to the destination: between two atoms (bond forming) or onto an atom (that atom keeps the electrons).

arrows.heading: Arrow types
points: Full (double-barbed) arrow = a PAIR of electrons moves. Polar mechanisms.
Fishhook (single-barbed) arrow = ONE electron moves. Radical mechanisms, always in pairs.
Heterolytic cleavage (one full arrow) makes ions; homolytic cleavage (two fishhooks) makes radicals.

arrows.heading: Vocabulary
points: Nucleophile: electron-rich, donates a pair, attacks. Think 'nucleus-loving' — it seeks positive charge.
Electrophile: electron-poor, accepts a pair, gets attacked.
Leaving group: departs with both bonding electrons. Good leaving groups are weak bases (I⁻, Br⁻, tosylate).

orgopreview.heading: Substitution vs elimination at a glance
points: SN2: strong nucleophile + unhindered (primary) carbon. One concerted step, backside attack, inversion.
SN1: weak nucleophile + tertiary carbon + polar protic solvent. Goes through a carbocation.
E2: strong or bulky base. One concerted step, needs the H and leaving group anti-periplanar.
E1: weak base + tertiary + polar protic. Shares the carbocation step with SN1.

orgopreview.heading: What tips the balance
points: Substrate: primary favours SN2, tertiary favours SN1/E1 or E2. Secondary gives mixtures.
Bulky base (KOtBu) → E2, because it cannot reach for backside attack.
Polar protic (water, alcohols) → SN1/E1. Polar aprotic (DMSO, acetone) → SN2.
Heat favours elimination (more particles, higher entropy).

orgopreview.heading: Carbocation stability
points: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl, from hyperconjugation and alkyl donation.
Resonance beats that ranking: an allylic or benzylic primary cation can outdo a plain secondary one.
Carbocations rearrange (hydride and methyl shifts) to reach a more stable arrangement — watch for it in SN1/E1.

energy.heading: Two separate questions, never confuse them
points: ΔG (thermodynamics) asks: is this FAVORABLE? Negative ΔG = products favored = large Keq.
Ea (kinetics) asks: is this FAST? Bigger barrier = slower, no matter how favorable.
A reaction can be strongly favorable and still take years. Diamond → graphite is the standard example.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Exothermic (−ΔH) helps; increasing disorder (+ΔS) helps, and helps more as T rises.

energy.heading: Reading a reaction coordinate diagram
points: Peaks = transition states = one per step. Count peaks to count steps.
Wells between peaks = intermediates (carbocations live here). They are real but short-lived.
Transition states sit at maxima and can never be isolated; intermediates sit at minima and sometimes can.
The rate-determining step is the one with the tallest barrier measured from the valley before it.
SN1 has two peaks and one well. SN2 has a single peak and no intermediate.

energy.heading: Rate laws are evidence for mechanisms
points: SN2: rate = k[substrate][nucleophile]. Both in the slow step → one concerted step → bimolecular.
SN1: rate = k[substrate] only. The nucleophile joins after the slow ionization, so it does not affect rate.
If doubling a reagent does not change the rate, that reagent is not in the rate-determining step.

energy.heading: Things that trip people up
points: A catalyst lowers Ea only. It never changes ΔG, Keq, or the products — just the speed.
Heat does not lower the barrier; it gives more molecules the energy to clear it.
Hammond postulate: an uphill step has a late, product-like transition state. This is why a more stable carbocation also FORMS faster.
Kinetic product = fastest to form (low temperature). Thermodynamic product = most stable (higher temperature, reversible).

isomers.heading: The isomer decision tree
points: Same molecular formula? If no, not isomers at all.
Different connectivity (what is bonded to what)? → constitutional (structural) isomers.
Same connectivity, different 3-D arrangement? → stereoisomers.
Interconvert by rotating a single bond alone? → not isomers, just conformations of ONE compound.

isomers.heading: Stereoisomers split in two
points: Enantiomers: non-superimposable mirror images. Identical physical properties; opposite optical rotation.
Diastereomers: stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images — including cis/trans pairs. Different physical properties, so separable.
A 50:50 mix of enantiomers is racemic and shows no net optical rotation. SN1 reactions produce these.
Meso compounds have stereocenters but an internal mirror plane, so they are achiral overall.

isomers.heading: Finding stereocenters
points: A stereocenter is a carbon with FOUR DIFFERENT groups. Two identical groups disqualifies it.
Compare groups all the way out, not just the first atom.
n stereocenters give at most 2ⁿ stereoisomers; symmetry can reduce that.

isomers.heading: Why alkenes have cis/trans and alkanes do not
points: Sigma bonds rotate freely, so alkane conformers interconvert constantly and are one compound.
A pi bond blocks rotation — breaking it costs far too much — so cis and trans are separable compounds.
Both alkene carbons must carry two DIFFERENT groups for cis/trans to exist.

isomers.heading: Isomers vs resonance — a common mix-up
points: Isomers are different substances you could put in separate flasks. Atoms are in different places.
Resonance forms are two incomplete drawings of ONE substance. Only electrons differ.
Tautomers (where an H actually moves) are isomers in equilibrium, drawn with ⇌, not ↔.

aminoacids.heading: The only five with charged side chains
points: Acidic (negative at pH 7.4): Aspartate (Asp, D) pKa 3.9, Glutamate (Glu, E) pKa 4.3.
Basic (positive at pH 7.4): Lysine (Lys, K) pKa 10.5, Arginine (Arg, R) pKa 12.5.
Histidine (His, H) pKa 6.0 — the borderline case, and the most important one. Near physiological pH it can gain OR lose a proton, which is why it appears in so many enzyme active sites.
Learn these five and the other fifteen follow by elimination: everything else is polar or nonpolar.

aminoacids.heading: Classifying by side chain
points: Carboxylate (–COO−) → acidic. Amine, guanidinium or imidazole → basic.
–OH, –SH, or amide (–CONH2) → polar uncharged: Ser, Thr, Cys, Tyr, Asn, Gln.
Pure hydrocarbon or aromatic with no polar group → nonpolar: Gly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Met, Pro, Phe, Trp.
Watch the amide trap: Asparagine and Glutamine are the NEUTRAL amides of the acidic Asp and Glu.
Tyrosine is aromatic but polar, because of its ring hydroxyl. Phenylalanine is the same ring without the OH, so it is nonpolar.

aminoacids.heading: The ones with special jobs
points: Glycine — side chain is just H. The only achiral amino acid, and the most flexible.
Proline — side chain rings back to the backbone nitrogen. Rigid, and breaks alpha helices.
Cysteine — two of them oxidize into a disulfide bridge, the only covalent crosslink in tertiary structure.
Methionine — always the first residue of a new protein (AUG is the start codon).
Tryptophan and Tyrosine — responsible for protein absorbance at 280 nm, which is how concentration is measured.

aminoacids.heading: One-letter codes that are not the first letter
points: R = Arginine, K = Lysine, D = Aspartate, E = Glutamate, N = Asparagine, Q = Glutamine.
F = Phenylalanine, W = Tryptophan, Y = Tyrosine.
The rest are the first letter: A, C, G, H, I, L, M, P, S, T, V.

buffers.heading: The one equation
points: pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]).
pH = pKa → equal amounts of acid and base (1:1). This is where buffering is strongest.
Each pH unit ABOVE the pKa multiplies base-to-acid by ten: +1 → 10:1, +2 → 100:1.
Each unit BELOW does the reverse: −1 → 1:10, −2 → 1:100.

buffers.heading: Protonated or not — the two-step check
points: Step one: is the pH below the pKa? If yes, the group KEEPS its proton. If above, it has LOST it.
Step two: work out what that means for charge. A neutral acid (–COOH) losing a proton becomes −1. A positive amine (–NH3+) losing one becomes neutral.
Worked example: aspartate side chain, pKa 3.9, at pH 7.4. pH is above pKa, so deprotonated, so −1 and negative.
Worked example: lysine, pKa 10.5, at pH 7.4. pH is below pKa, so protonated, so +1 and positive.

buffers.heading: Choosing and using buffers
points: Effective buffering range is pKa ± 1 pH unit. Outside that, one form runs out.
Pick the buffer whose pKa is nearest your target pH. Phosphate (7.2) and HEPES (7.5) are the standards for work near physiological pH.
A buffer needs BOTH a weak acid and its conjugate base present. A strong acid cannot buffer.
Blood holds pH 7.4 on bicarbonate (pKa ~6.1) only because it is an open system — the lungs blow off CO2, which keeps the ratio adjustable.

buffers.heading: Isoelectric point (pI)
points: The pI is the pH at which a molecule carries NO net charge.
For an amino acid with no ionizable side chain, average the two pKa values flanking the zwitterion: glycine is roughly (2.3 + 9.6)/2 ≈ 6.0.
Proteins are least soluble at their pI, which is what isoelectric precipitation and IEF gels exploit.

biomolecules.heading: One bond type per macromolecule
points: Proteins: peptide bonds (amides) between amino acids.
Carbohydrates: glycosidic bonds between sugars.
Nucleic acids: phosphodiester bonds between the 3-prime OH and 5-prime phosphate.
Fats: ester bonds between glycerol and fatty acids.
All four are built by condensation (releasing water) and broken by hydrolysis (consuming it).

biomolecules.heading: The four levels of protein structure
points: Primary — the amino acid sequence itself.
Secondary — alpha helices and beta sheets, held by hydrogen bonds between BACKBONE atoms only.
Tertiary — the whole chain folded in 3-D, held by SIDE-CHAIN interactions: the hydrophobic effect, H-bonds, salt bridges, and disulfides.
Quaternary — two or more separate chains assembled together.
Denaturation destroys shape but leaves the sequence intact, which is why a denatured protein is inactive but not chemically degraded.

biomolecules.heading: Why proteins fold at all
points: The hydrophobic effect dominates. Water must build an ordered cage around exposed nonpolar groups; burying them releases that water.
It is entropy-driven — and the entropy that increases is WATER's, not the protein's. This point is tested often and misremembered often.
Disulfide bridges are the only covalent contribution to tertiary structure.

biomolecules.heading: Nucleic acid quick facts
points: Nucleoside = base + sugar. Nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate.
Purines (two rings): Adenine, Guanine. Pyrimidines (one ring): Cytosine, Thymine, Uracil.
A–T has 2 hydrogen bonds; G–C has 3, so GC-rich DNA melts at a higher temperature.
RNA uses uracil in place of thymine, and ribose in place of deoxyribose.
